analysis.one_liner: Restores the phaseouts of personal exemptions and itemized deductions for high-income taxpayers.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on October 7, 2005 and never received a hearing, vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2001, Congress had scheduled the elimination of two tax provisions that raise taxes on the highest incomes: the phaseout of personal exemptions (which gradually removes personal exemptions as income rises) and the overall limit on itemized deductions (which shrinks itemized deductions for very high earners). This bill would cancel that scheduled elimination starting in 2006, restoring both phaseouts and making the limit on itemized deductions permanent. The effect is to collect more tax from the highest-earning households.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers as a whole, in the form of a more progressive income tax: the added revenue would come entirely from the highest-income households, the same households that benefit most from itemized deductions and large exemption amounts. The bill itself does not direct the new revenue to any specific program, so the benefit to working people is indirect, through reduced deficits or whatever future Congresses choose to fund.
analysis.who_benefits_short: General taxpayers, at high earners' expense

how_it_helps.text: The bill restores the personal exemption phaseout, under which high-income taxpayers gradually lose their personal exemptions as income rises, for tax years after 2005 [S3][S2].
It restores the overall limitation on itemized deductions, which shrinks itemized deductions for taxpayers above a high income threshold, and makes that limitation permanent [S3][S2].
The CRS summary describes the bill as repealing the scheduled elimination of both the exemption phaseout and the deduction limitation [S2].

analysis.who_pays: High-income households. Both phaseouts only affect taxpayers whose income exceeds high thresholds, so the entire cost of the bill falls on upper-income filers, particularly those who claim large itemized deductions or many personal exemptions.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not say what the additional revenue would be used for, so its benefit to ordinary taxpayers is indirect and depends on future fiscal choices [S3].

Phaseout rules are a complicated way to raise taxes on high incomes: they function as hidden rate increases that taxpayers may not understand, and a good-faith critic would prefer raising rates directly and transparently.
The change would take effect for the very next tax year, leaving high-income filers little time to adjust their withholding and estimated payments.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a straightforward progressive tax change: it shifts a modest amount of tax burden onto the highest earners by restoring two long-standing phaseouts that the 2001 tax law had scheduled to disappear. The cost is concentrated on a small group of high-income households, and the benefit to everyone else is diffuse, since the bill does not designate the new revenue. The main honest criticism is that phaseouts are an opaque way to raise rates and that the bill offers no plan for the money.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Finance Committee from the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress expired.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Harkin introduced the bill on October 7, 2005, joined by Senators Kohl, Levin, and Kennedy as cosponsors [S1][S3][S4].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, which handles all tax legislation [S5][S1].
No further action was ever taken on the bill; it never left the Finance Committee before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-income households came out ahead: because the bill died, the scheduled elimination of the exemption and deduction phaseouts continued, and the wealthiest taxpayers kept the lower effective taxes that the bill would have clawed back.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High-income taxpayers kept their tax cuts

for.name: Tom Harkin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to restore the exemption and deduction phaseouts.

for.name: Herb Kohl, Carl Levin, and Edward Kennedy

against.name: Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it in committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and with no Republican support the bill went nowhere in a Republican-controlled Senate; the record shows no votes on it at all [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill's entire cost would fall on filers above the phaseout thresholds, who would lose some personal exemptions and see large itemized deductions reduced. Its defeat preserved their lower effective tax rates.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax planning services
industries.note: Restoring the phaseouts would have added computational complexity that high-income filers often pay professionals to handle, a modest revenue loss for that industry had the bill passed.
